records.themeTitle: Israel’s sanctification gives expression to heavenly holiness
records.themeSummary: God sanctifies Israel and entrusts the sanctification of the month to them. Rav Tzadok reads the language of holiness above as something God chooses to establish through Israel’s holiness and praise.
records.originEnglish: This follows the Midrash there: the blessed God did not wish to sanctify it Himself, for that would be sanctification for Himself. Rather, He sanctifies Israel; because they are holy, what they sanctify becomes consecrated, like an ordinary vessel into which one places something holy. Therefore they sanctify it, as it says, ‘You shall be holy to Me, for I am holy.’ See Matnot Kehunah there; its explanation is strained. It seems that the meaning is: through your being holy, ‘I am holy.’ In this way they explained the teaching, ‘My holiness is above your holiness’: through your holiness, I am holy above. And it says, ‘You are holy, enthroned upon the praises of Israel’—established through Israel’s praises; see there.
records.targetEnglish: That is: kodesh, written without a vav, indicates the source of holiness, which does not need to receive holiness from another. Kadosh, written with a vav, indicates that it is summoned from kodesh: it must draw holiness from the source. It is unlike kodesh without a vav, which indicates holiness in its own right. As things appear, Israel are called kadosh with a vav, because they must draw holiness to themselves from its blessed source; kodesh would belong to the blessed God alone, the source of holiness. Yet because Israel surrender their entire grasp to God, it becomes clear that they arose in thought above the grasp of creation: their root is in the holiness that is higher than all, holy in its own right. Therefore it is written, ‘Israel is kodesh to the Lord.’ Moreover, through Israel’s service, a vav is drawn above, as the holy Zohar explains: when Israel sanctify, they raise the supreme glory from below to above, until the vav, the mystery of the upper heavens, ascends. When those heavens rise above, that kodesh shines into them, and then it is called kadosh above. The blessed God is called kadosh with a vav: God says that the honor of Heaven is, as it were, incomplete without Israel’s service, and only through Israel’s service will the honor of Heaven be completed.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim explains the apparent reversal in Rav Tzadok’s reading. Israel receive holiness from its source, yet their surrender and service disclose a holiness rooted above their present understanding. God chooses to describe the manifestation of heavenly honor as completed through that service. The passage’s ‘as it were’ is essential to the way it speaks of God’s holiness being established through Israel. This supplies the conceptual basis for entrusting sanctification to people.

records.themeTitle: Human differences give Oral Torah its particular expressions
records.themeSummary: The Written Torah supplies the light, and Israel illuminate through their innovations in Oral Torah. These innovations remain words of the living God, even while God credits the Sages with bringing them forth.
records.originEnglish: The blessed God illuminates through the light of the Written Torah, and Israel illuminate through Oral Torah, through what they innovate by analysis. In truth, these too are ‘words of the living God,’ as stated in Eruvin and likewise in Bava Batra; see Ramban there, who explains that this comes from the holy spirit and is higher than prophecy. Nevertheless, God entrusted it to the Sages as though they produce this light. Through ‘your light has come’—what God illuminates in their hearts—they shine before Him. Scripture first says, ‘Arise, shine,’ because in the visible expression they are the ones illuminating. Concerning this the Midrash says, ‘You yearn for the work of Your hands’: God yearns for them, that it be attributed to Israel that they are the ones who illuminate.
records.targetEnglish: Therefore the greater part of Torah is oral, as stated in Gittin. What is written encompasses all Israel, and all souls are equal in it: these are the general principles. In the particulars, however, they divide according to the particulars of the souls. Just as bodily healing differs with the constitutions of bodies and with changes between generations—what benefits this body or this generation will not benefit another—so it is with the healing of the soul. From this arose all the disagreements in Oral Torah: each spoke according to the level of his soul, identifying what was appropriate to its repair and healing. Therefore ‘these and those are words of the living God,’ for both were given by one Shepherd. The distinctions between the judgments correspond to the distinctions between the souls.
records.explanation: Sichat Malakhei HaSharet explains what the human contribution can add: the common principles of Torah take particular forms suited to different souls and circumstances. This illuminates how the Sages’ own analysis can be both their distinctive contribution and divine teaching. The surrounding discussion concerns the discernment of qualified Torah teachers; the comparison does not turn every private opinion into an equally authoritative ruling.

records.themeTitle: Shared holiness includes distinct roles in receiving and transmitting it
records.themeSummary: Although holiness belongs to all Israel, Rav Tzadok preserves gradations and the need to receive from Moses and Aaron. Aaron’s role is to make Torah’s illumination enduring in the heart.
records.originEnglish: At the revelation at Mount Sinai, all of them were at this level, as stated in Shir HaShirim Rabbah on ‘Let him kiss me.’ Afterward, although holiness permeates all Israel, there are nevertheless gradations, and they needed to receive from Moses and Aaron, as stated in Eruvin: ‘What was the order of teaching?’ Concerning this, Shemot Rabbah says: ‘Send Your light and Your truth’—these are Moses and Aaron, as it is written, ‘Your Thummim and Your Urim,’ and, ‘The Torah of truth was in his mouth.’ It then says, ‘This month shall be yours’; see there. This is the essence of the sanctification of the month entrusted to them: through it they illuminate the hearts of Israel. Moses our teacher is the root of Torah’s light, as it says, ‘She saw that he was good’: when he was born, the whole house filled with light. Its becoming permanently established in the heart comes through Aaron, the attendant of the Matronita, who draws people near to Torah. This is ‘the Torah of truth that was in his mouth,’ and a truthful lip endures forever.
records.targetEnglish: For Aaron, peace be upon him, was the one set apart from Israel, ‘to sanctify him as most holy.’ In him appeared the strongest revelation of the utmost holiness and separation that can be revealed in this world. Therefore he entered the Holy of Holies, the place of which it says, ‘No person shall be in the Tent of Meeting when he comes to make atonement in the holy place.’ Our Sages explained in the Jerusalem Talmud: even those whose faces have the likeness of a human face [the angels]. There is a holiness above that of the angels which they cannot reach; only the righteous can, whose place is further within than that of the ministering angels. Israel are ‘one nation,’ all together one complete stature. Yet, just as the human body has principal organs in which life is stronger, such as the heart, the source of life, so the other organs have different levels.
records.explanation: Yisrael Kedoshim gives Rav Tzadok’s distinction an organic form: Israel constitute one living whole, while its members have different capacities to receive and transmit holiness. Aaron’s special role belongs within that shared life. This helps explain why the holiness of the entire people is compatible with the need for Aaron to establish Torah in their hearts.

records.themeTitle: Rest can prepare renewed Torah when Torah remains within the heart
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok distinguishes the sleep of spiritual laziness from the sleep called ‘very good’: a short rest can enable renewed labor in Torah. Mar Cheshvan’s rising from a fall leads toward Kislev’s rectified sleep.
records.originEnglish: In Bereshit Rabbah it is taught: ‘Behold, it was very good’—this is sleep. They ask: is sleep very good? Rather, through sleeping a little, a person rises and labors greatly in Torah. In this way one repairs the fall itself: it becomes an aid to divine service, and one draws service from it. This is in the following month, Kislev, whose letter is samekh and whose attribute is sleep.
records.targetEnglish: Although everyone has a time of diminished consciousness, and it is impossible to remain always in expanded consciousness and the proper cleaving to God—as sleep was created and Bereshit Rabbah calls it ‘very good,’ because through it one rests and returns to receive fresh vitality—so too one must sometimes rest a little from words of Torah, and ‘the suspension of Torah is its foundation.’ Nevertheless, even at such a time, a person’s thoughts differ according to his level in the Torah that is upon his heart. Thus with our father Jacob: his dream, the images he experienced at the time of diminished consciousness, was also ‘Behold, the Lord stood over him.’ So it is with each person according to his level.
records.explanation: Tzidkat HaTzadik supplies a criterion for the distinction between restorative rest and abandonment. The Torah already rooted in a person continues to shape even the interval of diminished attention. This explains how the interruption itself can serve renewed life in Torah, while preserving Rav Tzadok’s requirement that it actually lead to renewed effort.
records.originHebrew: וְאִיתָא גַּם כֵּן בַּמִּדְרָשׁ (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה ט): "'וְהִנֵּה טוֹב מְאֹד' – טוֹבָה שֵׁינָה, וְכִי שֵׁינָה טוֹב מְאֹד וְכוּלֵי? אֶלָּא מִתּוֹךְ שֶׁהוּא יָשֵׁן קִימְעָא הוּא עוֹמֵד וְיָגֵעַ בַּתּוֹרָה הַרְבֵּה". וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁיְּתַקֵּן הַנְּפִילָה עַצְמָהּ שֶׁתְּהֵא לוֹ סַיַּיעְתָּא לַעֲבוֹדַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וּמִמֶּנָּה יִקַּח לַעֲבוֹד אֶת הַשֵּׁם. וְכֵן אַחַר כָּךְ בְּחֹדֶשׁ כִּסְלֵו: "הִמְלִיךְ אוֹת סָמֶ״ךְ בְּשֵׁינָה וְכִסְלֵו בַּשָּׁנָה".

records.themeTitle: Torah can give a fallen person the first strength to rise
records.themeSummary: The fallen sukkah of David does not mean the disappearance of divine kingship. God supports the fallen, and the fall can become a beginning of ascent.
records.originEnglish: The Gemara says there: nevertheless, David supported them through the holy spirit, as it says, ‘The Lord supports all who fall.’ It is also written, ‘the fallen sukkah of David,’ for a sukkah is a temporary dwelling. Thus, even when it appears fallen, he supports it, continually drawing the attribute of His blessed kingship into the world. The fall is for the sake of ascent, as it says, ‘A righteous person falls seven times and rises.’ Concerning the future it is written, ‘I will raise up the fallen sukkah of David.’
records.targetEnglish: The principal support of those who fall from their level comes through words of Torah, which give strength and sound counsel. This comes through truthful speech recognizing the greatness of the blessed God, even when the person is utterly distant from Him. Such is Torah: one is not standing before the King, so this is possible even during the fall and distance, and through it one is supported. Prayer, however, is like standing before the King, being close to Him; this is not possible at the time of the fall, since the person is not close. Even the prayer of the poor person from a broken heart is then impossible, for that too requires strength, and at the time of the fall the person lacks even this: the heart is completely blocked, like a stone. Concerning this they said, ‘Draw him to the study house; if he is stone … he shatters.’ Through words of Torah the person is supported and strengthened to awaken and rise from the fall.
records.explanation: Tzidkat HaTzadik describes how the first support can reach someone who cannot yet produce a feeling of closeness or even a brokenhearted appeal. Truthful Torah speech can precede that emotional renewal and restore the capacity to rise. This gives a concrete path to the support and renewed beginning urged in Mar Cheshvan. The contrast describes spiritual capacity in this condition; it is not a ruling that such a person should stop praying.

records.themeTitle: A fuller revelation calls for awe that restrains spiritual self-importance
records.themeSummary: The Temple makes the Divine Presence an enduring dwelling and thereby brings awe into the world. Rav Tzadok distinguishes this awareness of standing before God from fear of punishment.
records.originEnglish: In the Temple the dwelling was permanent, as it says, ‘Jacob called it a house.’ When there is a fixed place for the resting of the Divine Presence, awe comes into the world. It says, ‘So that you may learn to fear,’ which is not fear of punishment but true awe: through the revelation of the Divine Presence, awe enters the heart. Thus they said, ‘With great fear’—this is the revelation of the Divine Presence. As the Rema writes, when a person takes to heart that the great King stands over him and sees his deeds, fear and submission immediately come to him.
records.targetEnglish: The blessed God began building the fullness of the honor of heavenly kingship in the days of Abraham our father. With him God began to show that the honor of His kingship, as it were, reaches its complete fullness only through Israel’s service. In his days it began, as it is written, ‘The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord.’ The holy Zohar explains that this is why Jacob said, ‘How awesome is this place’: where fullness is found, awe is found. When God began to illuminate His will that without Israel’s service there would be no fullness in heavenly kingship, as it were, it followed that all this fullness was placed in Israel’s hands. Israel then needed to restrain themselves with great awe. Otherwise, God forbid, they could receive an excessive sense of power from this illumination, imagining that His governance was in their hands. God would then rise above this garment and show that nothing is in the person’s hands. Therefore, where fullness is found, awe is found.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim explains why a greater revelation produces a greater need for awe. Being entrusted with service that contributes to heavenly honor can itself invite self-importance; awe keeps the recipient aware of the Giver. This develops Rav Tzadok’s distinction between fear of punishment and the humility that accompanies awareness of the Divine Presence.

records.themeTitle: A season’s spiritual possibility depends on how its power is used
records.themeSummary: The Flood’s rain was first sent in mercy and could have become blessing through repentance. Rav Tzadok reads Mar Cheshvan as a season for making the renewed flow of Torah permanent through accepting its yoke.
records.originEnglish: It says, ‘The rain was upon the earth for forty days’: God brought it down in mercy, so that if they returned, it would be rain of blessing, as Rashi explains. This is Torah, for the Gemara says, ‘Water means Torah.’ But because they did not return and corrupted their ways, it became raging waters, and that generation was judged; afterward it says, ‘The Flood was forty days.’ In Tishrei, ‘There was light’ is Rosh Hashanah, as stated in Tikkunei Zohar; likewise the Midrash explains, ‘My light’ on Rosh Hashanah. The renewal in Torah begins then, for ‘Torah is light,’ and continues until Shemini Atzeret, the flowing wellspring of Torah. Then the light of Oral Torah and its innovations are established. From that time, forty days are given to receive this flow and renewal in Torah permanently. So too, concerning the rainy season, the first rain, yoreh, is in Mar Cheshvan. Yoreh ‘instructs’ people to plaster their roofs and so forth; it also alludes to instructing people to accept the yoke of Torah in truth.
records.targetEnglish: At the time of a person’s failure, he should know that this very time is a preparation for that same matter for good. If he merits it at that moment, he can rise to a very great level. The greatness of the good he can receive then corresponds to the greatness of the sin toward which the inclination entices him—if he turns this longing and desire toward good. The good comes from that very matter, as the opposite of the evil. Thus the Zohar says that at the time of the Flood they were fit to receive Torah, and Moses was then present, as our Sages expounded the word beshaggam; see there. Water means Torah, but they turned it into ‘raging waters.’ Torah is the ultimate support of the world, for whose sake it was created, yet they caused its destruction. Had they merited it, that time was prepared for the very opposite: the descent of the waters of Torah to sustain the world. Likewise, at the time of the destruction the Messiah was born, as stated in the Jerusalem Talmud. That time was prepared, had they merited it, for the Messiah’s coming and the building of the eternal Temple. This was the error of the people of Jerusalem and the false prophets: they thought that, on the contrary, God would do good to them, because they saw that the time was prepared for this—if they merited it.
records.explanation: Tzidkat HaTzadik extends the Flood’s unrealized possibility to the individual: a powerful desire can be redirected toward a corresponding good. It also explains the condition in Rav Tzadok’s seasonal reading. A time being suited to blessing does not guarantee the result; the final example explicitly identifies the mistake of treating potential as a promise. Accepting the yoke of Torah is the response that the Mar Cheshvan passage calls for.

records.themeTitle: Restraint makes a vessel for rain to become blessing
records.themeSummary: Mar Cheshvan’s task is to accept the demanding work of Oral Torah. Through that response, the waters can become rains of blessing from Torah’s wellspring.
records.originEnglish: The task in Mar Cheshvan is to accept the yoke of Torah in truth. The essence of the yoke of Torah is in learning Oral Torah, which involves great exertion and loss of sleep; one who desires wealth and pleasure cannot acquire Oral Torah, as stated in Tanchuma, Noach. We learned, ‘Whoever accepts upon himself the yoke of Torah, they remove from him … .’ Therefore most harsh decrees threaten in this month, so that people will accept Torah in truth and the waters will become rains of blessing from the wellspring of Torah, as stated.
records.targetEnglish: From His side, the blessed God constantly pours forth every kind of blessing and good kindness, as it says, ‘The earth is full of the Lord’s kindness.’ The person, however, may lack a vessel to receive it, for the principal matter depends on the person’s vessel. If a person restrains himself in receiving God’s abundance, avoiding unbounded expansion with it and instead entrusting it to God, then God correspondingly limits His abundance so that it does not spread beyond the person’s vessel; consequently it is blessing. Thus the Sages ask why rain is called an expression of might: because it descends with force. God limits it so that it goes only where needed. But if a person expands himself with God’s abundance and does not recognize that God gave it to him, the abundance likewise spreads into wilderness and desolation, into alien places, and consequently becomes a curse. Even concerning the Flood generation, the Midrash says that if they had returned, the rain would have been rain of blessing. Because they expanded themselves without restraint in His abundance, God correspondingly expanded His abundance, and it became rain of curse. Yet from God’s side, God forbid, no curse ever arises, only blessing.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim supplies a mechanism for the change from destructive waters to useful rain. Restraint and recognition of the Giver make the recipient capable of receiving abundance within a fitting measure. This illuminates why Rav Tzadok joins the promise of rain to the yoke and exertion of Torah: disciplined reception gives the flow a form in which it can become blessing.

records.themeTitle: Awe preserves Torah by giving it authority over conduct
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok ties enduring wisdom to fear of God and to doing Torah for its own sake. Awe makes Torah’s words permanent in the heart.
records.originEnglish: The Midrash says: ‘By your lives, all wisdom and all Torah are one simple matter: whoever fears Me and performs the words of Torah has all wisdom and all Torah in his heart.’ It brings ‘The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord; good understanding belongs to all who perform them,’ ‘The fear of the Lord is pure, enduring forever,’ and ‘The fear of the Lord is wisdom.’ These three verses show that the essence of wisdom is fear of God and fulfilling Torah’s words. As the Gemara says, it does not say ‘those who study them,’ but ‘those who perform them’: those who act for its own sake, as it says, ‘Good understanding belongs to all who perform them.’ It brings ‘The fear of the Lord is pure, enduring forever,’ because through awe the words of Torah become permanently established, since fear of God endures forever, and the fear of the Lord is wisdom.
records.targetEnglish: Love of Torah is the level of Isaac, for it involves accepting a yoke, as stated in Berakhot concerning ‘Our leaders are burdened’: it resembles afflictions. Sanhedrin speaks of giving him a taste of commandments and afflictions. It is called ‘the yoke of Torah,’ like ‘the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven,’ which is awe. Torah has the same numerical value as yirat, ‘fear of,’ and Scripture calls it ‘The fear of the Lord is pure, enduring forever.’ The Sages continually say, ‘Moses received from the mouth of the Power,’ because Torah comes from the side of strength. Likewise, ‘Happy is the person who is always afraid’ is said concerning Torah, the level of ‘the fear of Isaac.’ This is why the Sages say that the Holy One brought down the dew of resurrection at the giving of Torah: resurrection comes from the side of strength, and is therefore mentioned in the blessing of divine might. Likewise, Torah limits a person’s conduct and manner of walking, in accordance with the attribute of strength.
records.explanation: Kometz gives the awe described in Mar Cheshvan a practical meaning: accepting Torah’s authority places limits on conduct. This connects the heart’s enduring wisdom with the earlier requirement to perform Torah for its own sake. Citation clarification: the displayed Hebrew edition places a Ta’anit 5a locator beside the dew at Sinai; the passage describing that revival is Shabbat 88b. The Hebrew quotation is preserved, and the clarified source is distinguished from that inherited locator.

records.themeTitle: Awe is the preserving restraint within spiritual growth
records.themeSummary: The words of Torah endure through awe. Rav Tzadok’s next movement joins that permanence to the rectification of the covenant and freedom from servitude.
records.originEnglish: The Midrash says: ‘By your lives, all wisdom and all Torah are one simple matter: whoever fears Me and performs the words of Torah has all wisdom and all Torah in his heart.’ It brings ‘The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord; good understanding belongs to all who perform them,’ ‘The fear of the Lord is pure, enduring forever,’ and ‘The fear of the Lord is wisdom.’ These three verses show that the essence of wisdom is fear of God and fulfilling Torah’s words. As the Gemara says, it does not say ‘those who study them,’ but ‘those who perform them’: those who act for its own sake, as it says, ‘Good understanding belongs to all who perform them.’ It brings ‘The fear of the Lord is pure, enduring forever,’ because through awe the words of Torah become permanently established, since fear of God endures forever, and the fear of the Lord is wisdom.
records.targetEnglish: This is like the Talmud’s teaching on ‘The fear of the Lord is his storehouse’: a person told his agent, ‘Bring a kor of wheat up to the attic.’ He brought it up, and the owner asked, ‘Did you mix a kav of humton into it?’ This is salty earth, through which the grain is preserved. Awe is like the action of salt in this world. The holy Ari explains that a person desires food because foods in the world seek to attach themselves to the human form, to be clarified, and they awaken the person’s desire for them. ‘A salt land that cannot be sown and does not produce’ requires restraint in a person; through salty earth the grain too is preserved. Likewise, through the restraints a person places upon himself, the existence of the human form is preserved. The principal restraint is circumcision. Therefore, when Abraham our father fulfilled the commandment of circumcision, he brought merit to all Israel after him, so that they could receive all the powers of good found in this world and all the powers of holiness. They would not be harried and swallowed up under the rule of idolaters, but would ‘bring what they have swallowed out of their mouths.’
records.explanation: Beit Yaakov explains permanence through the image of grain and its preservative. Restraint does not produce the grain, yet it enables the good already received to endure. The passage then connects that restraint to circumcision and the capacity to receive holiness without being swallowed into another power. It therefore illuminates both Rav Tzadok’s claim that awe preserves Torah and the adjoining discussion of covenant and servitude.

records.themeTitle: Joseph’s trial clarifies what his brothers could only suspect
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok reports the brothers’ suspicion that Joseph’s accusations reflected a fault of his own. Their suspicion stands within a discussion of Joseph’s purity, temptation, and sale into servitude.
records.originEnglish: The tribes suspected that Joseph was not free of this blemish, because he said that they cast their eyes upon the daughters of the land, as stated in Bereshit Rabbah. They knew that they themselves were clean of this and supposed that he was blemished in it, for whoever disqualifies others does so through his own blemish. For this reason they sold him as a slave. Whoever repairs this blemish in this month, which is suited to it, will be saved from servitude. The principal repair is through the attribute of awe and fear, which is the task of this month, as stated.
records.targetEnglish: ‘Come, let us sell him to the Ishmaelites.’ The tribes initially judged Joseph liable to death because he brought an evil report about them to their father. In their eyes this was a sin at the root of his life, God forbid: he was separating them from their father, and appeared to them to be separating the unity of the Holy One with the congregation of Israel. Jacob was then the righteous foundation of the world, upon whom the world rested, representing God in this world, and they comprised all Israel. They were all included in the word ‘one’ in the Shema: aleph corresponded to Jacob, het to the eight sons of the principal wives, and dalet to the four sons of the handmaids. In their judgment, Joseph wished to separate this unity. But Judah wisely said that the judgment was not settled: perhaps Joseph was good, and they were the ones mistaken about him. He therefore advised them to sell him, meaning: let us not do anything to him with our own hands; let the blessed God clarify him. If he is good at his root, God will certainly save him from every sin even in Egypt, and no outcast will remain cast away. God therefore clarified and refined him through the episode of Potiphar’s wife. The covenant of the sexual organ corresponds to the covenant of the tongue. When he was found clear in this, he also cleared himself of their suspicion concerning evil speech: he was innocent.
records.explanation: Mei HaShiloach keeps the brothers’ judgment explicitly uncertain and reads the later trial as the clarification of Joseph’s innocence. This helps the reader preserve Rav Tzadok’s distinction between what the brothers suspected and what was true of Joseph. It also explains how the trial involving the covenant addresses the earlier accusation involving speech, joining the section’s opening account of purity to its account of the sale.

records.themeTitle: The study house strengthens the work of redirecting desire
records.themeSummary: The counsel is to draw the inclination itself to the study house, directing its energy toward delight in Torah and the joy of its discussion. The study house is where Oral Torah is renewed.
records.originEnglish: The counsel is ‘Draw him to the study house’: let him place the desire in words of Torah, for this is why the inclination was created—to desire delight in Torah. So it will be in the future, when the inclination remains only for delight in Torah, as stated in Midrash HaNe’elam: without the evil inclination there would be no joy in Torah discussion. Likewise, Tanchuma says that the Holy One said, ‘You make it evil.’ The blessed God created the inclination as zeal for Torah, so that there would be joy in Torah discussion. This is ‘Draw him to the study house,’ the place of innovations in Oral Torah.
records.targetEnglish: They said, ‘Draw him to the study house,’ rather than simply saying that one should go and study on one’s own. They could also have said, ‘Draw him to words of Torah.’ Although all words of Torah are like fire, it is known that some fire is especially strong, great, and intensely burning, while other fire is small and weak. So it is with the levels of Torah. In the study house, Torah is taught to others, there is the Torah study of the community, and a great person is presumably present. Such Torah acts more powerfully because its fire is stronger. This is the meaning of ‘Therefore those who rule say: Come to Heshbon’: those who rule over their inclination. Only those rulers who have already burned the evil inclination within their bodies through the fire of Torah can act through their words upon the hearts of those who hear them.
records.explanation: Divrei Soferim develops the precise setting of Rav Tzadok’s counsel. The study house adds communal learning and the speech of a teacher whose Torah has worked upon his own inclinations. This explains why bringing desire into that setting can be more effective than relying on isolated effort, and gives practical content to the paragraph’s final emphasis on the renewal of Oral Torah.

records.themeTitle: The energy of desire can serve Torah while its evil form disappears
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok says that the inclination was created for delight in Torah. Its future role is the joy of learning, which clarifies the present work of redirecting its passion.
records.originEnglish: The counsel is ‘Draw him to the study house’: let him place the desire in words of Torah, for this is why the inclination was created—to desire delight in Torah. So it will be in the future, when the inclination remains only for delight in Torah, as stated in Midrash HaNe’elam: without the evil inclination there would be no joy in Torah discussion. Likewise, Tanchuma says that the Holy One said, ‘You make it evil.’ The blessed God created the inclination as zeal for Torah, so that there would be joy in Torah discussion. This is ‘Draw him to the study house,’ the place of innovations in Oral Torah.
records.targetEnglish: God established His will through garments, so that each thing is a garment for another. To the extent that a garment recognizes how it clothes His will, His will truly encompasses it as well. So many garments unfolded in the world that darkness clothed light, as the holy Zohar says: there is no service of the Holy One except from within darkness. There is good in the world, and there is what is called evil; there is also kelipat nogah, in which good and evil are mixed. Through great concealment, something from it can be brought into holiness, as we find that descendants of Haman learned Torah in Bnei Brak. Even the worst garment is also a garment for light, as it says there: there is no light except what emerges from darkness, no service of the Holy One except from darkness, and no good except from evil. Recognition of light’s excellence comes only through darkness. Thus the Sages say, ‘Without the evil inclination, there would be no joy in Torah discussion.’ The evil too is a garment. Yet evil itself will be completely annulled in its own apprehension, as Tikkunei Zohar says, ‘The serpent was naked beyond all’—naked, without a garment. This completely evil garment is called the serpent, and it will be entirely annulled because it does not recognize at all that it is only a garment for light. This is what Abimelech asked Abraham: ‘If you deal falsely with me, my child, and my grandchild’—a father’s compassion for his child extends this far. He asked that his apprehension not be utterly annulled, but that he at least be brought in as some garment for holiness, like ‘Without the inclination, there would be no joy in Torah discussion.’ Thus the inclination is a garment for holiness, through which there can be joy in Torah discussion.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim explains the distinction within the claim that the inclination will remain. Its capacity can become a garment through which the joy of Torah appears, while the evil that treats itself as independent is annulled. This sharpens the work described in Mar Cheshvan: retain and redirect the power of desire, with its purpose and allegiance changed.
